cards.text: Psalm 123 is a song of ascents. There's no name on this one, just somebody who needs help and knows exactly which way to look. Not down at the phone, friend, UP.

cards.question: In Psalm 123, where does the singer lift up his eyes?

answers.text: To the One enthroned in heaven
To the gates of the temple

cards.text: He doesn't just say he's looking up. He paints a picture of HOW he's looking.

cards.question: What picture does the singer use for the way his people's eyes are on the LORD?

answers.text: Farmers watching the sky for rain

cards.text: A servant watching the master's hand, and a maidservant watching her mistress's hand. I KNOW that look, friend, because every time Mother Miller reached toward that counter, I was holding my breath going PICK ME, PICK ME, PICK THE STAMPER.

cards.question: The singer pictures himself like a servant watching a master's hand. So how does he see the LORD?

answers.text: As the Master he depends on
As a friend who owes him a favor
As a judge he has to avoid

cards.question: The singer says his people's eyes stay on the LORD their God. How long will they keep looking?

cards.text: Then the waiting turns into asking, and he asks twice: 'Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy'. Once is a knock on the door, but twice? That's somebody who is NOT going home until that door opens.

cards.question: The singer begs the LORD for mercy twice. Why do his people need it?
The singer says his people have endured much scorn from the ___.
True or false: Psalm 123 ends with the LORD answering and the scorn stopping.

cards.text: Psalm 123 stops right there, with the proud still sneering and the singer's eyes still up. Sometimes that's the whole prayer, friend: look up, and keep looking.
Psalm 124 is another song of ascents, and this one is from David, Israel's king. He opens with a big what-if, so big he wants a whole crowd saying it with him.

cards.question: What's the big what-if David opens Psalm 124 with?

answers.text: If the LORD had not been on our side
If the walls had not stood strong
If the king had not stood firm

cards.question: David says: If the LORD had not been on our side, let ___ now declare.

cards.text: Then David says that line again, and this time he adds when: when men attacked them and their anger flared. It's like telling a friend about a near miss in traffic, you never say it just once: 'That truck was RIGHT THERE. Friend. RIGHT. THERE.'

cards.question: If the LORD hadn't been on Israel's side when angry men attacked, what does David say would have happened?

answers.text: They would have been swallowed alive
They would have scattered to the hills
They would have been taken captive

cards.text: Then David changes the picture. No more attackers.

cards.question: In David's new picture, what would have come over Israel without the LORD on their side?

cards.text: Floods, a torrent, raging waters. David says it three ways, like a friend telling you about last night's storm: it rained, it POURED, it came down SIDEWAYS.

cards.question: True or false: In Psalm 124, David says the floods really did sweep Israel away.

cards.text: Then the what-ifs are over, and David starts blessing the LORD.

cards.question: David blesses the LORD for something He did NOT do. What is it?

answers.text: Give them as prey to their teeth
Hand them as spoil to their swords
Leave them as chaff for the wind

cards.text: Now David gives one more picture of how they got out.

cards.question: What does David say Israel escaped like?

answers.text: A bird from the fowler's snare
A deer from the hunter's bow
A lamb from the lion's mouth

cards.question: In David's picture of the bird in the fowler's trap, how do they get free?

cards.text: The net tears, and the bird is GONE. I know that feeling, friend: years in the back of a junk drawer, then one night it slides open and BOOM, I'm out of there.
Then David closes the whole song with one line about where their help comes from.

cards.question: At the end of Psalm 124, where does David say Israel's help is?

answers.text: In the name of the LORD
In the strength of their king

cards.question: True or false: David's last line calls the LORD the Maker of heaven and earth.

findings.problem: The joke makes up a new detail about Papa Dorin's past: that he held his breath on the Millers' counter, hoping Mother Miller would pick him. The backstory says he was part of every batch. The holding-your-breath moment belongs to the drawer, not the counter. The rule only lets jokes make up small moments around his bakery.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: The question tells the baker the singer is like a servant watching a master's hand. The right answer then repeats the word 'Master', so it stands out. The wrong answers ('a friend who owes him a favor', 'a judge he has to avoid') don't fit that picture at all.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: This story card has 3 sentences: 'Then the waiting turns into asking... have mercy'.', 'Once is a knock on the door, but twice?' and 'That's somebody who is NOT going home until that door opens.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The wrong answers 'humble' and 'faithful' don't make sense as people who heap scorn, so they read as silly and the right answer 'arrogant' stands out.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The card says Psalm 123 ends 'with the proud still sneering'. Psalm 123:4 says 'We have endured much scorn'. It doesn't say whether the scorn is still going on. The text leaves that open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The card uses 'the singer's eyes still up' (Psalm 123:1-2) and the proud (Psalm 123:4), but it cites only Psalm 123:4.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The card only recaps the ending that card 11 already asked about, plus a reflection. It doesn't carry the baker forward through the passage.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop: 5 of 7 choice cards are multiple choice, with 1 fill in the blank and 1 true or false.

rule.text: They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: 'No more attackers' says the floods are separate from the attackers. The text never says how the flood picture connects to the men who attacked. Psalm 124:6 goes right back to 'their teeth'.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The card retells the torn net and the escape that cards 13 and 14 just asked about, then adds a joke. It tells no new part of the passage.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop: 7 of 10 choice cards are multiple choice, with 1 fill in the blank and 2 true or false.

rule.text: They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.
